subject: Keep unique values that are not explicitly in `group_by`

messages.author: 9c9b5f9c6aaa025d
messages.subject: Keep unique values that are not explicitly in `group_by`
parts:
Hi,
I am in the process of converting some old plyr code over to dplyr and I came across a situation that I solved in plyr that I can’t figure out how to do in dplyr, so I appreciate some help.

I often find that I have data frames that have multiple columns that are uniquely tied to a type of value. For instance, a value might have an ID, a name, a color, a size, etc. What I typically want to do is aggregate over that value, but keep all of the unique identifiers of that value (so I don’t have to rejoin tables after each aggregation).

I often have many of these values, so simply using them in `.` or `group_by` did not seem very efficient, so I solved this in plyr by using `colwise` with `unique`. Is there a similar approach I could use in dplyr? I saw `summarize_each`, but I couldn’t figure out how to get that to work.

Here is an example of what I am talking about:

library(dplyr)
df <- data_frame(
Value.ID = c(rep(123, 2), rep(456, 3), 789),
Value.name = c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 3), "C"),
Quantity = c(2,3,3,1,3,2))

# This is my current code that works using plyr
plyr::ddply(df, plyr::.(Value.ID), function(df){
new_df <- plyr::colwise(unique, function(v){ return(length(unique(v)) == 1) })(df)
new_df$Quantity <- sum(df$Quantity)
return(new_df)
})

# Works, but is missing the Value.name column
df %>% group_by(Value.ID) %>% summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))

# Works, but I have a lot of these values, so I don’t really want to have to hand-type each one
df %>% group_by(Value.ID, Value.name) %>% summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))

# Does not work. Using a similar idea to `select` using `:` would help, but is some cases
# might not solve things well if the columns are not all next to each other
# df %>% group_by(Value.ID:Value.name) %>% summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))

Thanks,
Doug

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: Keep unique values that are not explicitly in `group_by`
parts:
Doug, 

I was trying to figure something similar out using filter on multiple columns using the same criteria in a local RUG list. In the end I wasn't sure the response was all that great, but it did work. Essentially, create a character vector of your variable names and paste the entire call together. 

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/davis-rug/6BDJ82nW2s8

eval(parse(text = paste("df.clean <- df %>% filter(ID > 5) %>% filter(", paste(names(df)[2:6], "> 10", collapse = ", "), ")", sep = "")))

HTH
Brandon

messages.subject: Re: Keep unique values that are not explicitly in `group_by`
parts:
In my opinion both of these examples illustrate that non-standard
evaluation is painful and causes more problems than it solves[1]. Both
Doug's problem as well as Jane's example that Brandon linked to are
easy to solve using the standard evaluation versions:

df <- data_frame(
Value.ID = c(rep(123, 2), rep(456, 3), 789),
Value.name = c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 3), "C"),
Quantity = c(2,3,3,1,3,2))

df %>%
group_by_(.dots = grep("Value", names(df), value=TRUE)) %>%
summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))

df.names <- c("ID", paste0("x", 1:10))
df.names
df <- data.frame(matrix(sample(1:110), nrow = 10, ncol = 11))
names(df) <- df.names
filter_(df,
.dots = c("ID > 5",
paste(names(df)[2:6], "> 10")))

Moral of the story: nse makes things harder. My advice is to ignore it
and use group_by_, filter_ etc. everywhere.

Best,
Ista

[1] At lease at the user level. vignette("nse") suggests that it
simplifies thing for the package developers. Though it's hard to
understand how this is true given that they now have standard
evaluation versions of everything, so they have to write each function
twice. I've long wished they would drop the nse versions, as it makes
many things seem very difficult.

Hi Ista,
I generally agree with you that nse should be avoided. But FYI, your solution does not quite solve the problem I have. In my actual data, there is not necessarily a common term (e.g., "Value") on which to `grep`. The condition I want to use for keeping a column is that, after grouping, every value is the same, i.e., `unique` returns a single element. In my original example, I used `ddply` with `colwise` to achieve that but am having trouble finding a more elegant solution using `dplyr`.

Cheers,
Doug

messages.subject: Re: Keep unique values that are not explicitly in `group_by`
parts:
Hi Doug,

Sure, but the great thing about standard evaluation is that it works
with the rest of the R ecosystem. I'm trying to restrain my impulse to
rant, but this is another reason I really dislike the nse part of
dply: it encourages you to think as though you are locked into only
using dplyr functions. The inability to do groupwise processing that
returns anything besides a data.frame is another barrier. But once you
take care to avoid the non-standard evaluation parts of dplyr the rest
of R becomes useful again, so you can do something like

which_var0 <- function(D) {
names(D)[sapply(D, function(x) length(unique(x)) == 1)]
}

df %>%
split(df$Value.ID) %>%
lapply(FUN = which_var0) -> vnames

df %>%
group_by_(.dots = Reduce(intersect, vnames)) %>%
summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))

Best,
Ista

On Mon, Dec 22, 2014 at 11:36 AM, Doug Mitarotonda

<dougmit...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Ista,
> I generally agree with you that nse should be avoided. But FYI, your solution does not quite solve the problem I have. In my actual data, there is not necessarily a common term (e.g., "Value") on which to `grep`. The condition I want to use for keeping a column is that, after grouping, every value is the same, i.e., `unique` returns a single element. In my original example, I used `ddply` with `colwise` to achieve that but am having trouble finding a more elegant solution using `dplyr`.
>
> Cheers,
> Doug
>
>
>> On Dec 22, 2014, at 6:28 AM, Ista Zahn <ista...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> In my opinion both of these examples illustrate that non-standard
>> evaluation is painful and causes more problems than it solves[1]. Both
>> Doug's problem as well as Jane's example that Brandon linked to are
>> easy to solve using the standard evaluation versions:
>>
>> df <- data_frame(
>> Value.ID = c(rep(123, 2), rep(456, 3), 789),
>> Value.name = c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 3), "C"),
>> Quantity = c(2,3,3,1,3,2))
>> df %>%
>> group_by_(.dots = grep("Value", names(df), value=TRUE)) %>%
>> summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))
>>
>> df.names <- c("ID", paste0("x", 1:10))
>> df.names
>> df <- data.frame(matrix(sample(1:110), nrow = 10, ncol = 11))
>> names(df) <- df.names
>> filter_(df,
>> .dots = c("ID > 5",
>> paste(names(df)[2:6], "> 10")))
>>
>> Moral of the story: nse makes things harder. My advice is to ignore it
>> and use group_by_, filter_ etc. everywhere.
>>
>> Best,
>> Ista
>>
>> [1] At lease at the user level. vignette("nse") suggests that it
>> simplifies thing for the package developers. Though it's hard to
>> understand how this is true given that they now have standard
>> evaluation versions of everything, so they have to write each function
>> twice. I've long wished they would drop the nse versions, as it makes
>> many things seem very difficult.
>>
>> On Mon, Dec 22, 2014 at 8:53 AM, Brandon Hurr <brando...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Doug,
>>>
>>> I agree. It wasn't a very satisfying conclusion and it hurts readability
>>> severely but it gets what you want pretty well. I also wish that you could
>>> use similar structures for filter and the other functions.
>>>
>>> Brandon.
>>>
>>>
>>> On Sunday, December 21, 2014, Doug Mitarotonda <dougmit...@gmail.com>
>>> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Hi Brandon,
>>>> Thanks very much for your help on this. I will use your suggestion so I
>>>> can finish the replacement of my code, but hopefully there is a more simple
>>>> way to do this in the future.
>>>> Cheers,
>>>> Doug
>>>>
>>>> On Dec 18, 2014, at 3:13 PM, Brandon Hurr <brando...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Doug,
>>>>
>>>> I was trying to figure something similar out using filter on multiple
>>>> columns using the same criteria in a local RUG list. In the end I wasn't
>>>> sure the response was all that great, but it did work. Essentially, create a
>>>> character vector of your variable names and paste the entire call together.
>>>>
>>>> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/davis-rug/6BDJ82nW2s8
>>>>
>>>> eval(parse(text = paste("df.clean <- df %>% filter(ID > 5) %>% filter(",
>>>> paste(names(df)[2:6], "> 10", collapse = ", "), ")", sep = "")))
>>>>
>>>> HTH
>>>> Brandon
>>>>
>>>> On Thu, Dec 18, 2014 at 2:29 PM, Doug Mitarotonda
>>>> <dougmit...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Hi,
>>>>> I am in the process of converting some old plyr code over to dplyr and I
>>>>> came across a situation that I solved in plyr that I can’t figure out how to
>>>>> do in dplyr, so I appreciate some help.
>>>>>
>>>>> I often find that I have data frames that have multiple columns that are
>>>>> uniquely tied to a type of value. For instance, a value might have an ID, a
>>>>> name, a color, a size, etc. What I typically want to do is aggregate over
>>>>> that value, but keep all of the unique identifiers of that value (so I don’t
>>>>> have to rejoin tables after each aggregation).
>>>>>
>>>>> I often have many of these values, so simply using them in `.` or
>>>>> `group_by` did not seem very efficient, so I solved this in plyr by using
>>>>> `colwise` with `unique`. Is there a similar approach I could use in dplyr? I
>>>>> saw `summarize_each`, but I couldn’t figure out how to get that to work.
>>>>>
>>>>> Here is an example of what I am talking about:
>>>>>
>>>>> library(dplyr)
>>>>> df <- data_frame(
>>>>> Value.ID = c(rep(123, 2), rep(456, 3), 789),
>>>>> Value.name = c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 3), "C"),
>>>>> Quantity = c(2,3,3,1,3,2))
>>>>>
>>>>> # This is my current code that works using plyr
>>>>> plyr::ddply(df, plyr::.(Value.ID), function(df){
>>>>> new_df <- plyr::colwise(unique, function(v){
>>>>> return(length(unique(v)) == 1) })(df)
>>>>> new_df$Quantity <- sum(df$Quantity)
>>>>> return(new_df)
>>>>> })
>>>>>
>>>>> # Works, but is missing the Value.name column
>>>>> df %>% group_by(Value.ID) %>% summarize(Quantity = sum(Quantity))
>>>>>
>>>>> # Works, but I have a lot of these values, so I don’t really want to have
>>>>> to hand-type each one
>>>>> df %>% group_by(Value.ID, Value.name) %>% summarize(Quantity =
>>>>> sum(Quantity))
>>>>>
>>>>> # Does not work. Using a similar idea to `select` using `:` would help,
>>>>> but is some cases
>>>>> # might not solve things well if the columns are not all next to each
>>>>> other
>>>>> # df %>% group_by(Value.ID:Value.name) %>% summarize(Quantity =
>>>>> sum(Quantity))
>>>>>
>>>>> Thanks,
>>>>> Doug
